speaker_role: school financial aid officers (assistant directors of financial aid at University of St. Thomas, Minnesota)
commercial_incentive: None evident beyond promoting the university's own scholarships/aid office; informational session for prospective/current families.
key_insights: Breaks financial aid into gift aid (scholarships = merit-based, grants = need-based via FAFSA) versus self-help (work-study and loans that must be earned or repaid).

The main institutional scholarship requires no separate application -- the admission application itself is the scholarship application -- but many additional departmental and identity-based scholarships need separate applications with their own deadlines.
Recommends prioritizing outside/private scholarship searches locally before going national/global for better odds, and warns never to pay to search for or complete scholarship or FAFSA applications.

FAFSA computes an Expected Family Contribution (EFC) from income, assets, and household/college-enrollment counts, used to set grant, subsidized-loan, and work-study eligibility -- not necessarily the actual price a family will pay.

Advises always filing the FAFSA even if aid seems unlikely, since all dependent freshmen qualify for at least $5,500 in federal unsubsidized loans, and family circumstances (e.g., a second child in college) can shift eligibility.
Explains a 'special circumstance' process (opens around January) for families whose finances changed after the tax year used on the FAFSA, requiring supporting documentation submitted to a counselor.
Practical tips: use a personal (not school/work) email for FSA IDs since long-term access is needed, and use the IRS data retrieval tool to reduce the chance of being flagged for 'verification.'
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker (Neil) says the St. Thomas Scholarship can go up to $34,000 per year, renewable each of four years if enrolled full-time with a 2.0 GPA.
Speaker says all dependent freshmen qualify for at least $5,500 in federal unsubsidized loans regardless of financial need.
FAFSA priority deadline stated as December 1st with full aid offers targeted by mid-January; early action deadline November 1st with decisions by December 15th; enrollment deposit deadline May 1st.
notable_or_distinctive: Gives an unusually concrete, step-by-step institutional walkthrough of one school's aid process with specific dollar figures and deadlines rather than generic national advice.
reliability_notes: School-specific details (scholarship amounts, deadlines, process) apply only to University of St. Thomas and this admissions cycle; general FAFSA/EFC concepts are broadly applicable but should be checked against current-year FAFSA rules.
